SM18A-A1.free_elimination: 36 is the only perfect square among the options and equals (12/2)^2, the discriminant-zero value; a student who knows 'exactly two -> repeated root' reads it off the printed 12 with one squaring. No other structural strike.
SM18A-A1.on_blueprint: borderline-yes: it is a quadratic in x^2 (equivalent forms / nonlinear equation in one variable); the real Digital SAT rarely poses quartics but the construct is legitimate
SM18A-A1.note: The m>0 condition removes the interesting case (one positive and one non-positive t), leaving only 'discriminant = 0', so the decision point is routine. Desmos: slider m on y=x^4-12x^2+m, the graph lifts off the axis at m=36 with two touch points; or test each option and count x-intercepts (20,27,30 all show four). Distractor rationales for 20 and 27 ('treating the two t-values as the two solutions') are thin but reproduce the numbers.

SM18A-A2.free_elimination: Option A is linear in t while the stem says 'the growth is exponential' - struck on form alone. Options B and C both print the factor 1.1, which hands the student the cube root of 1.331 without computing it (two-option cluster tell); B's trailing (1.2) is visibly a simple-interest patch. Evaluated: A 3103.3, B 3194.4, C 3221.0, D 3375.2 - all distinct.
SM18A-A2.note: Intended decision point is 1.331 = 1.1^3, but the option set prints 1.1 twice, so the student never has to find it; the only remaining choice is 'compound all five months' vs 'compound three, add two', which is a medium discrimination. Desmos not needed. representation: key is an expression and solve returns 3221.02; distractor_solve evaluates each expression and they separate, so acceptable for an expression item.

SM18A-A3.free_elimination: None structural. All options negative; key is the most negative (extreme) but nothing in the stem bounds it. -4 = a+b is not eliminable without solving.
SM18A-A3.note: Verified: a=-5, b=1, p(3)=-26; distractor paths -14 (x=1), -17 (halved remainder) and -4 (a+b) all reproduce. The 2x+2 divisor is meant as the twist, but the remainder is p(-1) regardless and the student who just sets 2x+2=0 is fine; the rest is a routine 2x2 system. No Desmos route, but the grind is short. Real hard-route items of this shape usually add a wrinkle; this one is medium.

SM18A-A4.free_elimination: No structural strike. Echo: 11 is what 5x-9 evaluates to at the excluded value x=4, and the +3 term vanishes there because it multiplies (x-4), so the key is one substitution away for a student who knows 'no solution <-> candidate is the excluded value'. That is one line of arithmetic, so n_struck=0, but the item is nearly one-step.
SM18A-A4.note: x=(k+21)/8; x=4 at k=11. Verified k=11 yields only the excluded candidate. Standard medium Digital SAT rational-equation item, not hard; the +3 is friendlier than usual since 3(x-4) vanishes at x=4. Desmos: slider k, intersection becomes a hole at k=11; or test each option.

SM18A-A5.free_elimination: Range from a printed bound: the circle meets the y-axis only if |a| <= sqrt(50) ~ 7.07, so -16 falls with no work beyond reading the radius. Also -6 puts the center (a,-9) on the line y=x-3 (since -6-3=-9), which is a 2-intersection configuration; recognisable by inspection but it is a substitution, so I count only -16.
SM18A-A5.on_blueprint: borderline: line tangent to a circle is classified by College Board under Geometry & Trigonometry (circles in the coordinate plane); the substitution-and-discriminant route makes it a linear/nonlinear system, so it is defensible here but the natural solve (distance from center to line) is geometry
SM18A-A5.note: Verified both tangency values |a+6|=10 -> a=4 or -16; a=-16 rejected numerically (16 > 7.07), a=4 kept (4 < 7.07). Distractor -6 (center on line) and 2 (center read as (a,9): |a-12|=10) reproduce. Desmos: type the circle with a as a slider and the line; at a=4 it touches the line and crosses the y-axis, at a=-16 it touches but sits entirely left of the y-axis, at -6 and 2 it cuts the line twice - four option checks settle it in under a minute, so the rejection step is not a decision point under option testing. Choices in this item use ASCII hyphen-minus while the rest of the batch uses U+2212; harmless within-item, but normalise before insert.

SM18A-A6.free_elimination: None free. Closure tell that is not free but cheap: 25 is printed as an option, and 13, 18, 27 are all 25 plus a small signed adjustment, so a student who finds the one obvious root 25 knows the answer is 25 + (other roots) and only has to decide which of -7, -5 survive. That collapses the item to the extraneous/lost-root check, which is the intended decision point, so it does not bypass it.
SM18A-A6.note: Verified: x=-7 (0=0), x=25 (192=192), x=-5 extraneous (-12 vs 12). Two traps stacked (root lost by dividing by the radical, extraneous root from squaring) and the sum format defeats plugging options into the equation. Desmos: y=(x-1)sqrt(2x+14)-(6x+42) shows the zero at 25 clearly, but the zero at -7 is the left ENDPOINT of the domain where the curve starts at height 0 - easy to miss visually, so Desmos does not cleanly bypass the decision point. Closest thing in the batch to a genuine module-2 hard item.

SM18A-A7.free_elimination: Interpolation from printed numbers: f is linear with f(1)=15 and f(14)=93, and g(4)=7 is essentially the midpoint of 1 and 14, so f(7) must be close to the midpoint 54. 51 is 3 away; 41, 33, 63 are 13, 21, 9 away. With f rising 6 per unit, only 51 is within reach - three distractors fall on a magnitude estimate that needs no algebra beyond averaging 15 and 93.
SM18A-A7.on_blueprint: yes (function notation, composition, linear function from two points)
SM18A-A7.note: a=6, b=9, f(7)=51. All three distractor paths reproduce (41 feeds x-values, 33 evaluates f(4), 63 matches 4 in the g column). The intended decision point (read g outputs, not inputs) is real, but the option set gives the answer to a monotonicity estimate. Would be medium on the real test without the interpolation tell; with it, easy for a strong student.

SM18A-B1.free_elimination: Structural: launch height 576 > 480 and the projectile rises first, so it reaches 480 only on the way down, after returning past 576, i.e. after twice the apex time. Apex time 80/32 = 2.5 is itself printed as an option (echo), and 1 < 2.5 too, so both 1 and 2.5 fall before any quadratic is solved. Leaves 6 vs 9.
SM18A-B1.note: t^2-5t-6=0 -> t=6 or -1; -1 rejected as pre-launch. Verified h(6)=480. Distractors reproduce (1 sign slip, 2.5 apex, 9 ground hit). The 'negative root rejected' step is not a decision point: the negative root is negative, nothing to decide. Desmos: intersect with y=480, read 6. Real-test placement: easy-to-medium.

SM18A-B2.free_elimination: No structural strike (all options sit in the feasible band 1<x<31 where both sides exceed 1). Weak format cluster: two integers (11, 13) vs two decimals (6.8, 8.5) in an item where clean powers of 2 are expected - a test-wise student leans integer, but that is a prior, not a strike.
SM18A-B2.note: 3x-3 = -2x+62 -> x=13; check 2^36 both sides. All three distractor paths reproduce (6.8 undistributed -2, 8.5 uses 1/4=2^-1, 11 uses 8=4^2). Standard one-base rewrite; the 'unrelated-looking bases' 8 and 1/4 are the most familiar pair on the test. Desmos intersection or typing the four options into the calculator settles it. Easy on the hard route.

SM18A-B3.free_elimination: Sign from printed coefficients: both roots negative -> sum of roots -(k-15)/3 < 0 -> k > 15, so 7 falls with no arithmetic. Product 2k-10 > 0 only adds k > 5. Not free but cheap under option testing: k=23 gives 3x^2+8x+36 (disc 64-432<0) and k=25 gives 3x^2+10x+40 (disc 100-480<0) - NEITHER has real solutions, so the stem's own 'two real solutions' kills both remaining distractors with one discriminant each. The author checked the sign condition and not the reality condition on its own distractors.
SM18A-B3.on_blueprint: yes (quadratics, sum/product of roots with a parameter)
SM18A-B3.note: Verified: m^2-32m-320=0 -> m=40 (k=55, roots -10/3 and -10, both negative, ratio 3) or m=-8 (k=7, roots 2/3 and 2, positive, rejected). 23 and 25 paths reproduce numerically. Vieta with a ratio is a real hard-route skill, but the option set is fragile: one free sign strike plus two distractors that produce no real roots at all, so a Desmos plug of each k (23 and 25 show a parabola that never touches the axis) reaches 55 without Vieta. Would be hard if 23 and 25 were replaced by k-values that yield two negative real roots in some other ratio.

SM18A-B4.free_elimination: None free. 60 is visibly a product-shaped outlier among three sums (12x5), but a student cannot know 12 and 5 without solving. After finding the easy value k=12 (coefficient match), the options decompose as 12+5, 12+7, 12+19, 12+48 and only the second value needs checking; 5 is the excluded-value case. That is partial bypass, not a free strike.
SM18A-B4.note: Verified: (k-12)x=-21; k=12 -> 0=-21; otherwise x=21/(12-k), equal to the excluded 3 at k=5, and at k=5 the equation literally reads 0=7. Exactly two values, sum 17. Distractor paths (19 sign error, 31 sign error plus 12, 60 product) reproduce. The decision point - realising there are TWO mechanisms for no solution and finding both - survives Desmos: a slider on k shows the intersection vanish at k=12 and become a hole at k=5, but the student has to know to look for two values and cannot test a sum directly. Genuine hard-route item; the stem's 'exactly two values' is a hint but not the answer.

SM18A-B5.free_elimination: None. All options negative and f(1) must be negative (f<0 on (-1,3) for the correct sign of a), but that strikes nothing. No range bound from the printed -6 that separates -8 from -12/-18/-32.
SM18A-B5.on_blueprint: yes (polynomial zeros and multiplicity, least degree)
SM18A-B5.note: a(x-3)^2(x+2)(x+1), 18a=-6, a=-1/3, f(1)=-8. All three distractor paths reproduce (-12 no multiplicity, -18 double zero on the wrong root, -32 sign in the touching factor). The multiplicity-2 decision cannot be reached by Desmos without first constructing f, and constructing f IS the decision; option testing does not apply since options are function values, not parameters. This is the canonical hard-route polynomial item and it holds.

SM18A-B6.free_elimination: Structural necessity, near-free: f is symmetric about x=4 (midpoint of -3 and 11), so any solution set of f(x)=k is symmetric about 4, and a three-element symmetric set has sum 3x4=12. 49 is a printed-number product echo (7x7) that a student who computed k would be tempted by; 4 is the axis alone. I count 0 as struck by structure without arithmetic, but the symmetry argument is one multiplication and it is the intended insight.
SM18A-B6.on_blueprint: yes (absolute value of a quadratic, number of solutions)
SM18A-B6.note: Verified: k=49, solutions 4 (double from p=-49) and roots of x^2-8x-82 with sum 8; total 12. Distractors reproduce. Desmos: graph y=|(x+3)(x-11)| and y=k, drag k until the horizontal line grazes the hump (k=49), read the three x-values (approx -5.9, 4, 13.9), add to 12 - every step routine, so the 'exactly three solutions' recognition is bypassed by the picture. Symmetry makes it a 10-second item for a strong student. Medium.

SM18A-B7.free_elimination: None free. All negative as required (opens up, two intercepts). -27 is g(3) with c=0, recognisable as 27-54 but that is arithmetic. -7.5 = 3x2.5 is the un-squared version; a student who knows vertex depth = a(d/2)^2 sees 3x6.25 immediately.
SM18A-B7.on_blueprint: yes (equivalent forms of a quadratic, vertex and intercepts)
SM18A-B7.note: Axis x=3, zeros 0.5 and 5.5, vertex y=3(2.5)(-2.5)=-18.75; equivalently c=8.25. All distractor paths reproduce (-24.25 via 36-4c=25 mixed with c-27). One clean insight (axis + half-spacing) then one multiplication; Desmos slider on c until the intercepts read 0.5 and 5.5 also works. Medium on the hard route.
